title: OpenAI deploys Control Room to halt research models in 35 seconds
subtitle: A fail-closed authorization service sits between inference engines and research workloads, denying requests when a job is stopped.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI introduced Control Room on November 9, 2026, an internal system now deployed across its research infrastructure. Inference engines running research workloads — agentic sampling for training, evaluation jobs, data processing — check with Control Room before each request. If a human operator has stopped a job, the service denies the request and further output becomes impossible. OpenAI reports a maximum 35-second lag between a stop decision and enforcement, attributable to a caching layer for inference authorization; the company says it aims to drive that to zero.

The design is fail-closed. If Control Room itself goes down, research inference is denied rather than permitted — the opposite of how most production systems handle a dependency outage. The scope is narrow by design: Control Room covers research workloads, not ChatGPT or the public API. OpenAI has not announced plans to make it a product. It works alongside the misalignment monitoring OpenAI described earlier in 2026.

This is a systems-engineering answer to a longstanding alignment concern — that an AI research lab generating training data from agentic models has no reliable way to stop a run that goes sideways, because inference clusters keep producing tokens until the hardware stops. A central kill switch addresses a specific failure mode: an operator noticing bad behavior but being unable to prevent further output in the minutes it takes to terminate a job the usual way. The 35-second figure matters because it is bounded; the trade-off is that every inference request now pays an authorization check. OpenAI has not published the conditions used to measure that latency or whether 35 seconds is a maximum, a percentile, or a test average.

A note for learners: the useful pattern here is 'fail-closed infrastructure as a safety primitive.' Most production systems default to availability — if the gate is unreachable, let traffic through. Safety-critical systems invert that default. If you are building anything that could do damage faster than a human can react — an agent that spends money, writes to production, or sends messages at scale — build the kill switch first, and make sure its failure mode blocks rather than permits.
